analysis.one_liner: Bans application and background-check fees and caps late fees for renters in federally backed housing.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 24, 2025 with 27 Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in House committees with no vote; in December it was sent to a subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells federal regulators to ban landlords from charging renters application fees and fees for background and credit checks, and to cap late fees at under 3% of monthly rent and only after rent is 15 days late. It also requires landlords to disclose the full monthly cost, their litigation history with tenants, ongoing pest and maintenance problems, and the rent increases of the past 10 years before a lease is signed. It applies only to rentals connected to federal housing programs or federally backed mortgages — FHA, VA, USDA, or loans bought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac [S2]. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and Federal Trade Commission would also have to define 'junk fees' in rental housing and block landlords from reporting unpaid junk fees to credit bureaus [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Renters applying for or living in federally assisted or federally financed housing. They would stop paying application and screening fees, face smaller and later-assessed late fees, and learn the true monthly cost and the landlord's track record before signing a lease [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits owners of covered units from charging any fee for submitting a rental application or for criminal history, tenant screening, consumer report, or other background checks [S2]
Caps late fees below 3% of monthly rent and bars them until 15 days after rent is due, with the limits disclosed in the lease [S2]

Requires landlords to disclose the total monthly amount due including fees, past litigation with tenants, ongoing pest and maintenance issues, and each of the last 10 years' rent increases before a lease is signed [S2]

Directs the CFPB and FTC to define rental 'junk fees' within 180 days and treat reporting unpaid junk fees to credit bureaus as an unfair debt collection practice under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Landlords of covered units — owners of federally assisted housing and properties with FHA, VA, USDA, or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac-backed mortgages — lose application and screening fee revenue and late-fee income, and take on new disclosure duties [S2]. Tenant screening companies lose a fee that landlords currently pass through to applicants [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only units tied to federal assistance or federally backed mortgage loans; renters in most market-rate apartments with no federal mortgage connection get none of these protections [S2]

Landlords lose application, screening, and late-fee income; an honest supporter would acknowledge some may offset this through higher base rents, and that screening costs still exist even if they can no longer be charged to applicants [S2]

Rules must be issued separately by four different regulators (HUD, VA, USDA, and the Federal Housing Finance Agency) plus the CFPB and FTC, which could mean slow, uneven implementation across housing programs [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters in covered units the gains are concrete and the costs are modest: junk fees disappear at signing and late fees shrink. The main weakness is coverage — the bill helps only renters whose housing touches a federal mortgage or assistance program, leaving most market-rate renters uncovered. The cost to landlords is real but small relative to rent, and the disclosure rules add paperwork rather than direct expense.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, and in December 2025 was sent to a subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxwell Frost introduced the bill on June 24, 2025 with 21 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S2]
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee and the Veterans' Affairs Committee on the day of introduction [S4]
It has 27 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S3]
On December 19, 2025 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity of the Veterans' Affairs Committee, its only movement in six months [S4]
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the record through the end of 2025 [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's situation has changed: landlords and tenant screening companies continue charging application, screening, and late fees, while renters in covered units keep paying them. With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action, the bill's current trajectory is typical of a minority-party bill that waits out the two-year Congress without a vote. If it does not advance before January 2027, it dies and would need to be reintroduced from scratch.

for.name: Rep. Maxwell Frost
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Junk Fees for Renters Act on June 24, 2025 [S1]

for.name: 27 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican cosponsored it [S3]

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; chair Rep. French Hill (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 24, 2025 and took no recorded action — no hearing or markup — leaving the bill untouched [S4]

against.name: House Committee on Veterans' Affairs
against.role: Second committee of referral; chair Rep. Mike Bost (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and, after six months, sent the bill to its Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity rather than advancing it [S4]

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a Democrat (27 of 217 House Democrats, zero of 223 Republicans), and both committees that hold the bill are run by the Republican majority.

industries.industry: Landlords of federally assisted or federally financed rental housing
industries.note: They lose application fees, screening fees passed to applicants, and late fees above the 3%/15-day cap, and must disclose rent history and litigation. These fee revenues come directly out of renters' pockets, so the industry's interest runs against tenants here.
Landlords can no longer charge applicants for criminal history and consumer report checks, eliminating a pass-through fee that today raises the cost of even applying for an apartment.
The bill would make reporting unpaid rental junk fees to credit bureaus an unfair debt collection practice, cutting off one way fee debts damage renters' credit.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in a subcommittee with 27 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, in a House controlled by the opposite party. Bills at this stage — no hearing, no markup, no floor schedule — very rarely advance before the Congress ends in January 2027; the most likely path is that it never gets a vote and expires.
